{{Short description|Space in topology mathematics}}
[[File:Marked 2-rose.svg|thumb|class=skin-invert-image|A wedge sum of two circles]]
In [[topology]], the '''wedge sum''' is a "one-point union" of a family of [[topological space]]s. Specifically, if ''X'' and ''Y'' are [[pointed space]]s (i.e. topological spaces with distinguished basepoints <math>x_0</math> and <math>y_0</math>) the wedge sum of ''X'' and ''Y'' is the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] of the [[Disjoint union (topology)|disjoint union]] of ''X'' and ''Y'' by the identification <math>x_0 \sim y_0:</math>
<math display="block">X \vee Y = (X \sqcup Y)\;/{\sim},</math> <!-- NOTE: In expressions like "a\sim b", the symbols \sim, being a binary relation symbol, has a certain amount of space before it and after it.  In this present expression, that spacing is not appropriate, and so it is avoided by enclosing "\sim" in curly braces, thus: "{\sim}". -->

where <math>\,\sim\,</math> is the [[equivalence closure]] of the relation <math>\left\{ \left(x_0, y_0\right) \right\}.</math>
More generally, suppose <math>\left(X_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> is an [[indexed family]] of pointed spaces with basepoints <math>\left(p_i\right)_{i \in I}.</math> The wedge sum of the family is given by:
<math display="block">\bigvee_{i \in I} X_i = \bigsqcup_{i \in I} X_i\;/{\sim},</math>
where <math>\,\sim\,</math> is the equivalence closure of the relation <math>\left\{ \left(p_i, p_j\right) : i, j \in I\right\}.</math> 
In other words, the wedge sum is the joining of several spaces at a single point. This definition is sensitive to the choice of the basepoints <math>\left(p_i\right)_{i \in I},</math> unless the spaces <math>\left(X_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> are [[Homogeneous space|homogeneous]].

The wedge sum is again a pointed space, and the binary operation is [[associative]] and [[commutative]] (up to homeomorphism).

Sometimes the wedge sum is called the '''wedge product''', but this is not the same concept as the [[exterior product]], which is also often called the wedge product.

==Examples==
The wedge sum of two circles is [[homeomorphic]] to a [[figure-eight space]]. The wedge sum of <math>n</math> circles is often called a ''[[bouquet of circles]]'', while a wedge product of arbitrary spheres is often called a '''bouquet of spheres'''.

A common construction in [[homotopy]] is to identify all of the points along the equator of an <math>n</math>-sphere <math>S^n</math>. Doing so results in two copies of the sphere, joined at the point that was the equator:
<math display="block">S^n/{\sim} = S^n \vee S^n.</math>

Let <math>\Psi</math> be the map <math>\Psi : S^n \to S^n \vee S^n,</math> that is, of identifying the equator down to a single point. Then addition of two elements <math>f, g \in \pi_n(X,x_0)</math> of the <math>n</math>-dimensional [[homotopy group]] <math>\pi_n(X,x_0)</math> of a space <math>X</math> at the distinguished point <math>x_0 \in X</math> can be understood as the composition of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> with <math>\Psi</math>:
<math display="block">f + g = (f \vee g) \circ \Psi.</math>

Here, <math>f, g : S^n \to X</math> are maps which take a distinguished point <math>s_0 \in S^n</math> to the point <math>x_0 \in X.</math> Note that the above uses the wedge sum of two functions, which is possible precisely because they agree at <math>s_0,</math> the point common to the wedge sum of the underlying spaces.

==Categorical description==
The wedge sum can be understood as the [[coproduct]] in the [[category of pointed spaces]]. Alternatively, the wedge sum can be seen as the [[Pushout (category theory)|pushout]] of the diagram <math>X \leftarrow \{ \bull \} \to Y</math> in the [[category of topological spaces]] (where <math>\{ \bull \}</math> is any one-point space).

==Properties==
[[Van Kampen's theorem]] gives certain conditions (which are usually fulfilled for [[well-behaved]] spaces, such as [[CW complex]]es) under which the [[fundamental group]] of the wedge sum of two spaces <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> is the [[free product]] of the fundamental groups of <math>X</math> and <math>Y.</math>
